player.concept: a quick-witted half-elf ranger with a longbow, a dry sense of humour and a soft spot for underdogs

established: Sewn into the lining of Prout's left boot was a page razored from the Royal Granary Roll: a dozen grain wagons for the King's Road this past month marked 'lost to goblins', each countersigned 'J. Sallow, for the Royal Purveyor', with Prout's pencilled note beside each of what the same wagon weighed at the river warehouses two days later, and at the foot: 'Not goblins. transcript.speaker: gm
transcript.text:
Wendell Prout turns slowly above the shut loft door, a pigeon hunched on the hoist beam beside him. Below, a scrawny boy in enormous black boots lobs gutter stones at the body. “Spin, you dead ink-pot! Cob’s got better aim than the hangman!” On the wall, a sharp-faced girl swears at him in Common, then spits a dockside curse after a passing pigeon.

A woman in a rain cape steps away from the gate, notebook in hand. “Sergeant Agnes Kell, investigator. The Captain calls it suicide. I haven’t written that down.” Her eyes flick to your hands, then back to your face. “Where would you like to start?”

transcript.speaker: player
transcript.text: I study the slowly turning body for a long moment, then turn to Kell. "Start? At the top, Sergeant. That is where he finished." I raise a hand toward the boy without looking at him. "You there, with the boots. Stop that at once. Every stone you throw alters the rate at which he turns, and the rate at which he turns is evidence." I squint up at the body and begin counting under my breath. "How many times has he gone round since you got here, lad? Be precise. A man is hanging on your answer."

transcript.speaker: gm
transcript.text:
Cob stops mid-throw, stone clenched in his fist. “Cob’s not your lad, and he ain’t counting for you.” He glances at Moll, who gives him a sharp look.

Kell’s mouth twitches. “A precise answer would be useful. But the boy’s got no clock.” She taps her pencil once against her notebook. “And the body’s turning because the wind’s at it, investigator—not because he’s keeping count.”

Moll kicks her heels against the wall. “He jumped, if you’re collecting answers. Midnight. Wailing about his debts. I saw the whole thing.”

Cob makes a rude noise and hefts the stone again, though he doesn’t throw it. The body turns another slow fraction above you.

transcript.speaker: player
transcript.text: I turn to the girl on the wall with grave courtesy and take out a stub of pencil. "A witness. Splendid. You say he jumped. Up, or down?" I wait, pencil poised. "Because if he jumped down, he jumped from somewhere, and the only somewhere up there is the loft door. Which is shut." I point at it. "Now. A man who jumps out of a door must first open it. And a man who has just been hanged is in no position to close it behind him. So either the door shut itself out of tact, or somebody else was up there." I make a careful note. "Also, you said wailing. Proper wailing, or just mentioning his debts loudly? It matters." I glance at the pigeon on the hoist beam. "Do not go anywhere, you. You are next."

transcript.speaker: dice
transcript.text: Insight check to see through Moll's story about the jump: 11 + 3 = 14 vs DC 13: success

transcript.speaker: gm
transcript.text:
Moll’s smile falters at your questions. Her eyes flick to the shut loft door, then to Cob. “Wasn’t there,” she mutters. “Couldn’t’ve seen it. It rained all night.”

Kell’s pencil pauses. Moll’s fist closes tighter.

“Fine,” Moll spits. “A gentleman paid me a silver crown at first light to say I saw him jump. There. Happy?” She opens her fist just enough to show the wheat-ear stamped on the coin, then hides it again. “He had a fine coat. A silver-topped cane.”

Kell writes carefully. “A paid lie. Noted.” She looks from the coin to the hanging clerk. “Who was he, and what did he want buried with Prout?”

transcript.speaker: player
transcript.text: I nod gravely to Moll. "Thank you. A paid lie is still evidence. It tells us someone thought a lie was worth a crown." Then I walk beneath the hoist beam, clear my throat, and address the pigeon with full formality. "Sergeant, please record this. Witness statement, the pigeon on the hoist beam." I look up at it. "You were present on that beam last night, or at least you are present now, which in the absence of a better witness I shall treat as the same thing. Did you see a gentleman with a fine coat and a silver-topped cane? Coo once for yes, twice for no." I wait, perfectly serious, pencil ready.

transcript.speaker: gm
transcript.text:
The pigeon blinks, gives one dry coo, and lifts off the beam in a burst of grey wings. It circles the yard once and settles on the granary roof, having declined to testify.

Kell watches it go. “Noted. An uncooperative witness.” She turns a page in her notebook. “We have a paid lie, a shut loft door, and a body hung where it couldn’t hang itself. Now we need the man with the cane—and a reason.”

Moll drops from the wall and catches Cob by the sleeve. He jerks away, one oversized boot scraping the cobbles. “Leave off,” he snaps, but his eyes dart toward the water butt. What do you do?

transcript.speaker: player
transcript.text: I raise a finger. "Sergeant, strike uncooperative. The witness cooed once. Once is yes. It confirmed the gentleman with the cane and then left before cross-examination, which is the privilege of witnesses with wings." I wait until she writes it, then turn to Cob. "Now, Cob. You looked at the water butt. A person looks at a water butt for one of two reasons: either it is interesting, or something is in it. I have examined that water butt from here, and it is not interesting." I walk over to it, roll up my sleeve, and peer in before reaching down into the water.

transcript.speaker: gm
transcript.text:
The water butt holds only rainwater and a skin of pigeon feathers. Your hand finds no hidden object—just cold water and the rough inner curve of the barrel.

Behind you, Cob edges toward it anyway. Moll catches his sleeve. “We’re going,” she says, eyes fixed on the gate.

Kell writes, “Pigeon: one coo; investigator interprets as affirmative.” She looks up at you. “I’ll allow it as a joke, not as proof.”

Cob’s borrowed boots scrape the stones. Something inside one gives a faint, papery crackle when he shifts his weight. Kell hears it too. “Those boots look dear for a boy who throws stones at the dead.”

transcript.speaker: player
transcript.text: I shake the water off my hand and glance up at the hanged man's feet, then down at Cob's. "Cob. Wait. Nobody is in trouble for the boots." I crouch to his height, perfectly solemn. "But boots do not crackle unless they have something to say. Your left boot has been trying to give evidence ever since I arrived, and you keep standing on it." I dig a coin from my purse and hold it up. "I am told the going rate for testimony in this yard is one crown. I will pay the boot the same, through you, its legal guardian. Take it off, and let it speak."

transcript.speaker: dice
transcript.text: Persuasion check to get Cob to name the men in the loft: 14 + 2 = 16 vs DC 12: success

transcript.speaker: gm
transcript.text:
Cob stares at the coin, then at you. “You said nobody’s in trouble for the boots.”

“I did,” Kell says, pencil still. “And I’ll stand by it.”

Something in Cob’s shoulders loosens. “They’re Mister Prout’s. Moll helped me get ’em off him.” He stamps the left one; paper crackles in its lining. “Two nights ago, I saw him sew something in there. And last night—” His voice drops. “Silvertop came up to the loft. The posh one with the silver cane. Came with the Purveyor’s wagons. Had his own key to the big doors. There was a big man with a bandaged hand, too.”

Moll’s grip tightens on his sleeve. Kell writes, slowly. “What happened up there?”

transcript.speaker: player
transcript.text: I press the coin into Cob's palm and close his fingers over it. "Fee paid. Go on, what happened up there? Take your time." I listen, then add thoughtfully, "A big man with a bandaged hand. Nobody bandages a hand that has done nothing. Hands that haul a rope over a hoist beam come away burned." I glance up at the beam, then hold out my own hand, palm up. "And then, Cob, the boot, if you please. I shall return it in the condition it was found, minus its testimony."

transcript.speaker: dice
transcript.text: Persuasion check to get Cob to name the men in the loft: 6 + 2 = 8 vs DC 12: failure

transcript.speaker: gm
transcript.text:
Cob’s fingers close around the coin, but he doesn’t take off the boot. At your mention of the bandaged hand, his eyes flash to Moll; her face has gone tight.

“Cob don’t know nothing,” he says, backing toward the water butt. The papery crackle stops as he plants his foot carefully. “And you said nobody was in trouble. So don’t go taking my boots.”

Moll moves between you and him, chin high, though one hand stays hooked in his sleeve. Kell doesn’t reach for either child. “He’s frightened, investigator,” she says quietly. “A coin isn’t the same as knowing he’ll be safe.”

transcript.speaker: player
transcript.text: I lower my hand and nod slowly. "The Sergeant is right. So let us be legal about it." I count it off on my fingers with great seriousness. "One. The King asked me to see Wendell Prout done right by. Two. Those are Wendell Prout's boots, and boots are part of a man's estate. Three. Therefore whoever is standing in them is standing in the King's business, and is under the King's protection until further notice." I look to Kell. "Further: the boots contain evidence. Cob is inside the boots. Cob is therefore evidence, and the Watch is obliged to keep evidence safe, dry and fed. Is that not so, Sergeant?" To Moll, quieter: "You too. You are holding the evidence by the sleeve. Nobody with a bandaged hand touches either of you. Where would you be safest tonight?"

transcript.speaker: dice
transcript.text: Persuasion check to get Cob to name the men in the loft: 9 + 2 = 11 vs DC 12: failure

transcript.speaker: gm
transcript.text:
Kell considers your argument, then gives a small, careful nod. “The King’s protection isn’t a charge I can enforce from here. But I won’t let anyone take them while I’m standing here.”

It isn’t enough for Cob. He retreats toward the water butt, Moll still at his side. “Cob don’t know nothing,” he mutters, guarding the boots with his hands. The fear in his face isn’t about the coin now; it’s about what happens after he talks.

Moll watches you closely. “Safe where?” she asks. “And safe from whom?”

transcript.speaker: player
transcript.text: I answer Moll as plainly as I can. "From whom: from Silvertop, and from whoever owns that bandage. Where: the palace kitchens. The King remembers how Prout took his tea. I expect he can learn how you take yours." I straighten up. "But you do not trust me yet, and you are right not to. So I shall demonstrate competence." I stride to the nearest pile of grain sacks by the granary wall, haul one onto my shoulder, and drop it beneath the hoist beam. "Sergeant, we are going to re-enact the crime. This sack is Wendell Prout. It weighs about what a clerk weighs, it has about as much to say, and it has the advantage of not having been murdered yet. If one big man with a rope can hoist it up there, so could he."

transcript.speaker: gm
transcript.text:
Kell’s gaze goes to the sack, then to your wet sleeve. “A sack won’t tell us who had the key, investigator. But it may tell us whether one man could manage the hoist.”

Before she can help, a boot scuffs behind you. Cob has edged to the water butt; now he stops, the left boot crackling sharply. “If I let you look in the boot, it stays mine,” he says, eyes on you. Moll studies your face, then adds, “And he stays with the sergeant. Witness, not prisoner.”

Kell opens her notebook. “While I’m here, yes. I’ll keep you both beside me.” She doesn’t promise beyond that. Cob lifts his heel a little, waiting for your answer.

transcript.speaker: player
transcript.text: "Agreed, on all counts. The boot stays yours. Its testimony goes to the Crown. You stay with the Sergeant, as a witness and not a prisoner." I offer Cob my hand and shake it firmly, then, for form's sake, bend and shake the toe of the left boot as well. "Contract sealed with both parties." Then I kneel, ease the lining open where the stitches are newest, and carefully draw out whatever paper Prout sewed in there, unfolding it so Kell can read over my shoulder.

transcript.speaker: gm
transcript.text:
Cob’s hand meets yours, then the boot’s toe. He watches your fingers pick at the fresh stitching, jaw tight, but doesn’t pull away.

The lining parts. A folded scrap slips into your palm, creased and crackling. The ink is cramped but legible: a list of grain wagons marked “lost to goblins,” each entry countersigned, “J. Sallow, for the Royal Purveyor.”

Kell leans close enough to read. Her pencil stops. “Prout came to the watch house three days ago,” she says, voice low. “Asked how to report false entries in the King’s rolls—and whether we could arrest a gentleman at the Purveyor’s office.”

Moll’s eyes dart toward the gate. Cob goes still. Kell turns to you. “This gives us a reason. Now tell me what you know about the man who paid her.”

transcript.speaker: player
transcript.text: I fold the list and hand it to Kell. "What I know of the man who paid her: fine coat, silver-topped cane, silver crown stamped with a wheat-ear, up and about at first light. A man who pays a child a whole crown for one lie is either very rich or very frightened, and in my experience a man with a silver cane is frightened of nothing but the price of silver. So: rich, and with something to lose. I would put a crown of my own on J. Sallow." I pick up my coil of rope. "Now. The sack." I loop a noose around the neck of the grain sack, toss the other end over the hoist beam beside Prout, set my feet, and haul, alone, counting each pull aloud for the Sergeant's notebook.

transcript.speaker: gm
transcript.text:
The cord pulls taut, and the sack rises—slowly, but steadily. The hoist creaks above you. Kell watches the line rather than the sack. “One person can work it,” she says. “That proves the hoist could lift him. Not that one person did.”

She looks down at the page in her notebook, thumb resting beside Sallow’s name. “Prout came to me three days ago. Asked how to report false entries in the King’s rolls. I sent him to the palace.” Her pencil presses a dark point into the paper. “I should have listened.”

At the name, Moll goes pale and clamps her fist shut. Cob stares at the page. “Silvertop,” he whispers. “That’s him.” Kell turns back to you. “What do you want written down?”
